voice.tone: Plain-spoken and confident without hype; explains reasoning directly and isn't afraid to name what's wrong with the old way
voice.rhythm: Short declarative sentences mixed with one longer explanatory one per paragraph; frequent one- or two-sentence paragraphs for emphasis
exemplars: We didn’t launch a new feature. We didn’t run any paid ads. We didn’t get a viral blog post or a lucky mention on Hacker News. What happened was much less dramatic than that. In late January, we spent a few days editing our homepage.

If you wanted to quickly figure out whether Plausible was worth trying, you had to scroll through an essay first. That’s not how people browse the web. People scan. They jump around and make snap judgments.

“Get started” is probably the most overused button label on the web. It tells you nothing about what happens when you click. Will it cost money? Is this a demo, a signup or a purchase? “Start free trial” answers the important part: this is a trial, not a commitment.

We didn’t remove all the prose. Plausible is not just a list of features, and we still want the homepage to explain why we exist. Our philosophy around privacy, simplicity and independence is a big part of what has kept us differentiated in the analytics market.

Google Analytics is frustrating to use, difficult to understand, slow to load and privacy-invasive. That's why we built Plausible Analytics, a simple, privacy-first alternative that doesn't cut corners.

segments.name: A founder or CTO of a small software company who switched everything off Google Analytics and now checks stats once a day in one minute
segments.situation: They run a product site plus a blog and a docs site. GA4 was installed years ago and nobody on the team can get a straight answer out of it any more — the reports that mattered are buried under menus, explorations and custom report builders. Someone on the team asked a simple question last week (which blog post is bringing signups?) and it took half an hour of clicking to half-answer it. Meanwhile the marketing site is carrying a cookie banner they never wanted, and the GA tag is one of the heavier things on a page they otherwise obsess over keeping fast. They have already looked at the alternatives; people they respect publicly say they moved. What they want is one page they can read in a minute and hand to a non-technical colleague without training.

objections.objection: Google Analytics is free. I am being asked to start paying monthly, per site, for something I already have at no cost.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence directly answers the free-versus-paid trade. The closest is a customer conceding the price and buying anyway — Cyrus Shepard's 'Not free and not a ton of bells and whistles, but SOOOO easy to use (for clients too)' — plus the low entry price ($9/month Starter, $14 Growth, 2 months free annually) and nonprofit/education discounts. The value case has to be made on the buyer's own time and compliance cost, which the evidence does not quantify. Treat this as unresolved with current evidence.

objections.objection: I have years of history in Google Analytics. Switching means starting from zero and losing every year-over-year comparison I have.
objections.answer: Historical Google Analytics data can be imported, and stats can also be brought in by CSV, so the switch does not begin with an empty chart. Period comparison then works against the imported range.

objections.objection: Installing and re-instrumenting tracking across my sites is a project I do not have time for right now.
objections.answer: Installation is one lightweight script, with a WordPress plugin, a Google Tag Manager template that needs no code change, and published guides for Shopify, Webflow, Squarespace, Wix, Next.js, Ghost and Hugo. Pageview goals — including the 'thank you' or order confirmation page — need no code changes at all, and scroll depth, outbound clicks, form completions, file downloads and 404s are tracked automatically. Only custom event goals require a snippet. One customer reports replacing a whole network of sites and paying within an hour of starting the trial.

objections.objection: Simple means underpowered. The moment I need a real answer — a funnel, revenue attribution, a segment, an API pull — I will hit a wall and have to keep GA anyway.
objections.answer: Funnels measure drop-off across a fixed sequence and user journeys let you work forwards from a page or backwards from a conversion; ecommerce revenue attribution assigns monetary values to goals; custom properties create custom metrics; saved and shared segments, period comparison, the Stats API (600 req/hour on Business), Events API, Sites API and a Data Studio connector all exist. The honest caveat comes from a customer: 'not a ton of bells and whistles'. Note that funnels, user journeys, custom properties, revenue attribution and the Stats API sit on the $19 Business plan, not the entry tiers.

objections.objection: The numbers will not match Google Analytics. When my client or my board sees different traffic figures, I am the one explaining the discrepancy.
objections.answer: Nothing in the supplied evidence reconciles Plausible's counts against Google Analytics or explains the gap. The only adjacent fact is built-in filtering of bots, referrer spam and data centre traffic, which is an argument for Plausible's numbers being cleaner but not an explanation of the difference, and no evidence quantifies it. This objection cannot currently be answered.

objections.objection: A team of ten with no investors. If they get acquired or shut down, my analytics — and my data — go with them.
objections.answer: Running since 2018, profitable, bootstrapped and self-funded, funded entirely by subscribers, with no outside investors and explicitly not an acquisition target. 21,000+ teams, 21k paying subscribers, 313B tracked pageviews, 99.99% uptime over 90 days, and the code is open source so customers are never locked in. Data can also be exported.

objections.objection: Without cookies you cannot really track individuals, so I lose returning-visitor identity, cross-device journeys and anything resembling real attribution.
objections.answer: This is accurate rather than deniable: no cookies, no persistent identifiers, no cross-site or cross-device tracking, by design. What is offered instead is UTM campaign tracking with automatic channel grouping, conversion attribution to referrer sources and entry pages, funnels, user journeys and ecommerce revenue attribution. No evidence in the ledger addresses the accuracy trade-off of cookieless measurement, so the individual-level loss is real and should be stated rather than argued away.

objections.objection: We already have GA4 configured, a consent banner deployed and a data layer someone built. Ripping that out is more disruptive than living with it.
objections.answer: The consent banner itself is the thing that goes away: no cookies, no personal data collection, no consent banners required, with GDPR, CCPA and data processing covered. Plausible can be deployed through Google Tag Manager without touching code, so it can run alongside the existing setup during evaluation rather than replacing it on day one.

objections.objection: I could self-host it. The code is open source, so why pay a subscription for something I can run on a box I already have?
objections.answer: The evidence confirms the code is open source and that customers are never locked in, but supplies nothing about the cost, effort or limits of self-hosting versus the hosted plans. There is no counter-argument available here beyond price ($9–$19/month) and the hosted operational record: 313B pageviews tracked, 99.99% uptime over the last 90 days.

objections.objection: Privacy is not a problem I have. I am not in the EU, nobody has complained, and 'no cookie banner' is not worth a line item.
objections.answer: For this reader privacy is the wrong lead. The non-privacy arguments are: a script 54 times smaller than Google Analytics, 135KB less JavaScript per visitor, one dashboard read in one minute with no menus or custom report building, real-time updating every 30 seconds, automatic scroll depth, AI-tool traffic from ChatGPT, Perplexity and Claude, and Search Console queries in the same dashboard. Compliance coverage (GDPR, CCPA) is there if it ever becomes their problem.

objections.objection: This is sized for hobby sites. With 10k pageviews on the entry plan and ten sites at the top of the self-serve tiers, it will not hold a real business.
objections.answer: It runs reliably from small sites to hundreds of millions of monthly visitors, with 313B pageviews tracked and 99.99% uptime over 90 days. Named users include Hugging Face, 37signals/Basecamp and Ghost. Above ten sites or ten team members, Enterprise adds 10+ sites and seats, 600+ Stats API requests per hour, Sites API access, SSO for Google Workspace / Entra / Okta, a managed proxy, scheduled raw event exports and priority support.

objections.objection: Nothing is on fire. I will look at this later.
objections.answer: There is no deadline in the evidence to create urgency, and nothing in the ledger documents a cost of waiting. What lowers the cost of acting now is the 30-day free trial with no credit card and no automatic charges, and a live public demo that can be inspected before signing up at all.

objections.objection: My data leaving my jurisdiction — or sitting with another US vendor — is the thing I am actually trying to avoid, and I cannot verify where it goes.
objections.answer: All visitor data is processed exclusively on servers owned and operated by European companies and never leaves the EU; Plausible is made and hosted in the EU on European-owned infrastructure. For Enterprise there is a managed proxy and scheduled raw event data exports.
